title: How Gratitude Makes Us, and Our Students, Better
author: Dave Stuart Jr.
summary: Stuart argues that gratitude is an underrated character strength that supplies the energy teachers and students need to do hard work. Drawing on a frightening week during his wife's sudden illness, he observes that a constant awareness of gratitude made loving action effortless, and he likens gratitude to a 'fusion reactor of willpower.' He then tells the story of Cabdul, a refugee student who arrived as the lowest reader in his grade and graduated in the top ten, crediting his relentless work to gratitude. The harder part, Stuart admits, is acting consistently on what we know. He illustrates this with his own late-night collapse into resentment, and suggests that habit-formation may be the key to turning character strengths from head knowledge into behavior. He closes by insisting that character work is worth continuing even though it is not a silver bullet, and that gratitude is 'more like a muscle than a merit badge.'
points: Stuart's central claim is that gratitude acts as a source of willpower, supplying energy for the relational, intellectual and creative work of teaching.
Cabdul's rise from lowest reader in his grade to top-ten graduate is offered as evidence that gratitude can drive grit and sustained effort in students.
He argues that knowing a character strength matters is not enough; the hard problem is turning it into consistent behavior.
Habit formation, drawing on Duhigg, is proposed as the way to make character strengths automatic and less effortful.
He warns educators against discarding good practices like character education just because they do not produce quick results.
quotes: This is because of gratitude, which acts like a fusion reactor of willpower, energizing us to do the work we need to do, whether it be the work of love or the work of teaching or the work of studying. I can't emphasize enough how important this is for us as teachers who want to teach well, who want their students to flourish in the long-term, and who want to lead good lives.

Doing the work we were born to do — the relational work, the intellectual work, the creative work, the Work Boots work — takes energy, which, for many of us teachers, is in short supply. Gratitude adds to that supply.

And yet, four years later, Cabdul graduated in the Top Ten of his class. The reason, from my observational and teacher perspective, was obvious: Cabdul had incredibly well-developed character strengths, things like grit and self-control.

Knowing isn't enough; it's the doing that counts. And while character strengths seem to be one heck of a promising sword in our battle to do the work of teaching as best we can, there's still so much we need to learn about helping our students (and ourselves) transform it from head knowledge to consistent behavior.

My hunch is that, for the folks who are gritty every day or self-controlled or socially intelligent, there's both a skill element and a habit element. The skill part enables them to do the skill; the habit part enables them to do it with less energy, less thought.
We can be too quick in education to throw things out that are actually quite good just because they didn't produce a desired result quickly enough (ahem, Common Core, maybe?).

Part of being a Never Finished teacher is realizing that failure is a normal part of growth. Gratitude is more like a muscle than a merit badge. You don't earn it; you develop it and then work to keep it in shape.
